title: John Napier and the Invention of Logarithms (1614)
explainer: In 1614 the Scottish mathematician John Napier published his Mirifici Logarithmorum Canonis Descriptio, introducing logarithms as a way to turn multiplication and division into simpler addition and subtraction. For three centuries afterward, engineers and scientists relied on log tables and slide rules built on this idea, long before electronic calculators existed. The same logarithm you're refreshing here reappears constantly in machine learning - in log-loss, cross-entropy, and the log-sum-exp trick used to keep probability calculations numerically stable - so it helps to see it as a 400-year-old shortcut for hard arithmetic rather than an arbitrary rule.

title: Zero as a Number: A Journey Through India, Arabia, and Europe
explainer: For most of ancient history, "zero" was only a placeholder symbol in positional systems (as in Babylonian numerals), not a number you could compute with. That changed in India: by the 7th century, Brahmagupta had written explicit rules for arithmetic with zero, such as zero plus zero equals zero, and Indian place-value numerals carrying zero later passed through the Islamic world into Europe. A math-literacy refresher is a good place to notice that treating "nothing" as a number with its own arithmetic was itself a hard-won mathematical idea, not something every civilization arrived at automatically.
